w: Call it the Venice of Africa: a third of this waterfront settlement stands on stilts above the lagoon, home to Egun fishing families who arrived from Badagry and Benin. Six villages, four of them floating. In 2012 the state demolished stilts beyond the power lines overnight, leaving families homeless.
s: The 'Venice of Africa' - a settlement built on stilts
_facts: A third of the community is built on stilts along the lagoon
Egun people from Badagry and Benin, main occupation fishing
Six villages: four floating (Adogbo, Migbewhe, Oko Agbon, Yanshiwhe), two on land
July 2012 demolition of stilts left many families homeless

w: Eleven-point-eight kilometres of concrete strung across the lagoon - Africa's longest bridge until Cairo's 6th October Bridge overtook it in 1996. President Shagari broke ground in 1980, Babangida finished it a decade later. A 2012 repair repainted it green-white-green, Nigeria's colours.
s: 11.8km of lagoon crossing, once Africa's longest
_facts: Was the longest bridge in Africa until 1996's 6th October Bridge in Cairo
Phase one commissioned by President Shagari in 1980, completed by Babangida in 1990
Measures about 11.8km, built by Julius Berger Nigeria
Repainted green-white-green after 2012 repair work

w: Founded in 1987, this charismatic megachurch once drew over 50,000 worshippers a week, beamed worldwide via its own channel, Emmanuel TV. Founder T.B. Joshua died in 2021 a global TV pastor; in 2024 the BBC reported allegations of abuse and torture under his leadership, and his widow took over as leader.
s: A global TV megachurch, and a 2024 reckoning
_facts: Founded 1987, over 50,000 attendees weekly at peak
Television network Emmanuel TV livestreams globally
Founder T.B. Joshua died 2021
2024 BBC reported allegations of abuse and torture by Joshua; widow Evelyn Joshua became leader

w: Balogun Market has no fixed address - it simply sprawls, block after block, across Lagos Island's streets. Traders here have built a reputation as the city's best source for fabric, shoes and just about anything else, a market too big to fit on any single map.
s: A market so big it has no fixed address
_facts: Sprawls across many streets on Lagos Island with no single address
Recognized as the best place to buy fabrics, shoes and wares

w: A 78-hectare pocket of conserved wetland and forest in the middle of fast-developing Lekki, part of the wider PARCC West Africa conservation project - a rare stretch of green held back from the concrete tide reshaping this corner of Lagos.
s: 78 hectares of reserve wedged into booming Lekki
_facts: 78-hectare Natural Resource Conservation reserve in Lekki
Part of the PARCC West Africa project

w: Seat of a monarchy older than the bridges and skyscrapers around it: the official residence of the Oba of Lagos, the city's traditional ruler, standing at the heart of old Lagos Island - a palace still doing the job it always has.
s: The Oba of Lagos still rules from here
_facts: Official residence of the Oba of Lagos
Situated on Lagos Island

w: Built in 1901 by the British colonial government, this was for decades the only bridge linking Lagos Island to the mainland - named for Governor Gilbert Carter. Independence came in 1960; the bridge itself was dismantled and rebuilt in the late 1970s, still doing the job it was built for.
s: Built 1901, once the only way onto the island
_facts: Built 1901, originally the only bridge connecting Lagos Island to the mainland
Named after Sir Gilbert Thomas Carter, Governor of the Colony of Lagos
Dismantled, redesigned and rebuilt in the late 1970s after independence

w: This Broad Street landmark carries the name of Madam Efunroye Tinubu - Yoruba slave trader, merchant and power broker whose influence shaped 19th-century Lagos. Once Ita Tinubu, it became Independence Square at Nigerian independence, then finally settled on the name of the woman herself.
s: Named for a slave trader turned power broker
_facts: Named after Yoruba slave trader, merchant and aristocrat Madam Efunroye Tinubu
Formerly called Ita Tinubu, then Independence Square after Nigerian independence

w: Nike Davies-Okundaye's five-storey gallery in Lekki holds around 8,000 works by Nigerian artists, making it one of the largest galleries in West Africa. It's the flagship of a small empire - sister branches operate in Abuja, Oshogbo and Ogidi - built entirely around one collector's eye.
_facts: Owned by Nike Davies-Okundaye, one of the largest galleries in West Africa
Collection of about 8,000 artworks from Nigerian artists, housed in a five-storey building
Branches in Abuja, Oshogbo and Ogidi

w: Once Her Majesty's Broad Street Prison, where activists who fought for Nigerian independence were held - now a memorial park designed by Theo Lawson, opened for the 50th independence anniversary in 2010. The old prison walls stayed; everything inside became a stage for concerts and quiet contemplation instead.
s: A colonial prison turned independence memorial
_facts: Formerly Her Majesty's Broad Street Prison, hosted political activists who fought for independence
Designed by architect Theo Lawson in 1999, built to commemorate the 50th independence anniversary in 2010

w: Lagos's first cable-stayed bridge, strung 1.36km across the lagoon to link Lekki with Ikoyi. Governor Babatunde Fashola cut the ribbon in May 2013, giving the city a rare piece of showpiece infrastructure - and locals a new favourite spot for a lagoon-side photo.
_facts: 1.36km cable-stayed bridge linking Lekki Phase 1 with Ikoyi
Commissioned 29 May 2013 by Governor Babatunde Raji Fashola

w: A Yugoslav architect built this 350-hectare trade complex in the 1970s, borrowing forms - the theory goes, per Rem Koolhaas - from Kano's architecture. It opened in 1977 for Lagos's first trade fair; by 2002 traders evicted from Balogun Market had colonised it, turning pavilions into fabric and auto-parts stalls.
s: A Yugoslav-designed trade city on 350 hectares
_facts: 350-hectare facility designed by Zoran Bojovic, built by Yugoslav firm Energoprojekt, opened 1977
Rem Koolhaas theorized Bojovic drew on architectural forms found in Kano
In 2002 traders from Balogun Market relocated there

w: Established in 1892 by Mohammed Shitta Bey, a Sierra Leonean-born aristocrat and philanthropist, this is one of the oldest mosques in southern Nigeria - and the first in the country to gain international recognition. It earned National Monument status in 2013, still doing its original job on Lagos Island.
_facts: Established 1892, one of the oldest mosques in Southern Nigeria
First internationally recognised mosque in Nigeria
Designated National Monument in 2013
Named after founder Mohammed Shitta Bey, Sierra Leonean-born aristocrat and philanthropist

n: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Lagos
w: Built in 1939 in full Gothic style, back when the Catholic church here was still just an apostolic vicariate - it took until 1950 for Rome to elevate it to cathedral, seat of the Archdiocese of Lagos. A slice of European ecclesiastical architecture holding its ground on Lagos Island.
s: Gothic seat of the Archdiocese of Lagos
_facts: Gothic-style building constructed in 1939
Elevated to cathedral status in 1950, seat of the Archdiocese of Lagos
